title: Savitri
hook: a childless king keeps offering with one verse, and the daughter he is given carries its name

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhari by the Ganga, asking only to see her sons, and for one night the dead rose without anger. Your line was Gandhari. Did you let one old quarrel rest, even in your own mind? Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

A verse with a second name. Earlier this year, the verse to the sun that people call the Gayatri turned up in the older law books under another name: the Savitri, the verse to the god Savitr. Keep that name in your pocket. In the Mahabharata, a sage sitting with the exiled Pandavas in the forest tells of a king who has no child, and the verse he keeps offering with is that one. Last year we heard Savitri's story from the first scene to the last. This time we stay with the woman herself, and we start where she starts: with her name.
screen: `THE GAYATRI HAS A SECOND NAME.` → `A KING WITH NO CHILD.` → `WHERE HER NAME CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: The king is Ashvapati, ruler of the Madras. The epic calls him good, truthful and generous, and it says he is grieved by one thing: there is no child in his house. So he takes up a discipline. He eats sparingly. He keeps his senses in check. And again and again, into the sacred fire, he makes offerings with the Savitri verse. The epic says he keeps this up a long time. Then one day the fire answers. The goddess Savitri herself rises out of it, pleased with him, and offers him a gift. He asks for children. She tells him a daughter will be born to him, full of radiance. And when the girl comes, the king names her after the goddess who gave her: Savitri. So a name that belonged to a verse, and then to a goddess, now belongs to a baby. Think about what the verse asks for. Earlier this year we heard it in paraphrase: may the sun god stir our thoughts. And the girl named for it grows into a woman who keeps her thinking clear under pressure. She is the one who goes out and chooses. She is the one who hears a terrible warning and doesn't flinch. She is the one who will stand in front of Death and keep talking. The epic doesn't spell out that link. It simply gives her the name and lets her grow into it. There's one more turn. The law books hang this verse on the edges of the day, dawn and dusk, said while the light is changing. Savitri's whole story happens at an edge like that, between a life and its end. A verse for the turning of the light, made into a woman who stands in the turning and keeps her head.
screen: `ASHVAPATI OFFERS WITH THE VERSE` · `THE GODDESS RISES FROM THE FIRE` · `THE DAUGHTER IS NAMED SAVITRI` · `A NAME TO GROW INTO`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with your own name. Settle, and let the breath slow down by itself. Bring to mind your name, said out loud by someone who loves you. Hear the voice. Who chose that name? What were they hoping for when they chose it? You don't need answers. Just let the questions sit. Then let the name go, and come back to the breath. If you know the Gayatri and you pray, you can say it once, silently, and let it finish before the bell. The bell holds the time.
Savitri. A princess named for the goddess who rose from the fire, and for the verse her father offered with. Today's word.
Your line: Savitri. Today, ask someone where their name came from, and listen to the whole answer, even the long version. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Hindus who keep the daily twilight rite, sandhya, recite the Gayatri, also called the Savitri, at dawn and dusk; Savitri's story itself is retold at home and in temple talks.

fork.setup: you're Ashvapati. after long years of offerings, the goddess Savitri rises from the fire and offers you a gift. what do you ask for?
fork.reveal: children. she promises him a radiant daughter, and he names the girl after the goddess.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the verse to the sun god Savitr, of the goddess who rose from the fire, and of the princess.

trapdoor: what you thought: Savitri is just the heroine's name.
what it means: she's named for the goddess who granted her birth, after her father's offerings with the Savitri verse.
what a scholar hears: one name on three things, a verse to Savitr, a goddess, and a woman who stands at the edge between life and death.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
